name: Fernando Meirelles
teaser: Meirelles made City of God with mostly untrained teenagers from Rio's favelas — the film's kinetic violence made it a global phenomenon and an Oscar nominee.

exploreAction.targetName: City of God (2002), the first 25 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the chicken, the chase, the freeze-frame of Rocket with a gun. Meirelles's camera is a whip: fast pans, rapid cuts, and a soundtrack that never pauses. Notice how the editing tells you who lives and who doesn't.

name: Walter Salles
teaser: Salles made Central Station about a letter-writer who helps a boy find his father — the film's performances by Fernanda Montenegro made it the face of Brazilian cinema worldwide.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the train station, the letter-writer, the crowd. Salles filmed in a real station with real passengers. Notice how the film's road trip slowly reveals the country through its people.

name: Glauber Rocha
teaser: Rocha led Brazil's Cinema Novo movement — he wrote a manifesto declaring that violence and hunger were the true language of Latin American film.

exploreAction.targetName: Black God, White Devil (1964), the first 25 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the sertão, the mysticism, the violence. Rocha's film is a fever of folk religion and revolution. Notice how the camera keeps the landscape and the people in the same frame — neither can escape the other.

name: Héctor Babenco
teaser: Babenco's Pixote follows a street child through the São Paulo juvenile system — the film is almost unbearably real, and its young star later lived a tragic real life.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the reform school, the children, the system. Babenco cast real street kids and filmed in real institutions. Notice how the film never lets the camera flinch — that's the point.

name: Alfonso Arau
teaser: Arau directed Like Water for Chocolate — a magical-realist romance where food literally carries emotion — and the film became the most successful foreign film in the US at its release.

exploreAction.targetName: Like Water for Chocolate (1992), the first 25 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the kitchen, the wedding, the recipes. Arau films cooking as magic: emotions enter the food and the food enters the diners. Notice how the film's recipes structure its chapters.

name: Alejandro Jodorowsky
teaser: Jodorowsky was a mime, puppeteer, and tarot reader before cinema — his El Topo and The Holy Mountain are psychedelic westerns that festivals had to explain to the public.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the gunslinger, the child, the desert massacre. Jodorowsky's western is a spiritual allegory wearing leather. Notice how the film's violence is always ritualistic, never realistic.

name: María Novaro
teaser: Novaro's Danzón follows a telephone operator who loses her dance partner and finds herself — the film is a love letter to Mexico's danzón dance halls.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the dance hall, the telephone exchange, the rhythm of two lives. Novaro films her heroine's freedom arriving through dance. Notice how the film's colors — teals, pinks, night blues — are choreographed too.

name: Ousmane Sembène
teaser: Sembène was a Senegalese dockworker and novelist before film — his Black Girl is widely considered the first feature film of sub-Saharan African cinema.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the apartment in Antibes, the 'gift' of employment, the isolation. Sembène films a domestic servant whose freedom was traded away. Notice how the mask she brings becomes the film's symbol of identity.

name: Djibril Diop Mambéty
teaser: Mambéty's Touki Bouki — a Senegalese Bonnie and Clyde fantasy — is famous for its two young lovers on a stolen motorbike, dreaming of Paris. It was restored to international acclaim decades later.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the slaughterhouse, the motorbike, the two lovers. Mambéty's editing is jazz: it cuts on rhythm, not story. Notice how the film's dream of Paris keeps colliding with Dakar's reality.

name: Abderrahmane Sissako
teaser: Sissako's Timbuktu was nominated for the Oscar — it tells of a family living under jihadist rule in Mali, filmed with tenderness and anger in equal measure.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the dunes, the family, the occupiers. Sissako films the desert as both refuge and prison. Notice how the film's most violent acts happen off-screen — restraint becomes accusation.

name: Youssef Chahine
teaser: Chahine was Egypt's greatest filmmaker — his Cairo Station (1958) is a noir thriller set among newspaper sellers, and his career spanned six decades.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the railway station as a small society, the newspaper sellers, the pin-ups. Chahine films obsession brewing in public. Notice how the station's crowds are both community and threat.

name: Nadine Labaki
teaser: Labaki's Capernaum told a street kid's lawsuit against his parents — she spent years researching with real street children, and the film was nominated for the Oscar.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the courtroom, the boy suing his parents, the flashback. Labaki cast a real refugee boy as the lead. Notice how the film's anger is always in service of the children.

name: Elia Suleiman
teaser: Suleiman makes 'Palestinian films without politics' — his Divine Intervention is a deadpan comedy where the joke is the occupation itself.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — Suleiman himself wordless, the traffic, the absurdity. His comedy is built on silence and stillness; the political horror arrives through the gaps. Notice how the film never once raises its voice.

name: Hany Abu-Assad
teaser: Abu-Assad's Paradise Now — about two friends recruited as suicide bombers — won a Golden Globe and an Oscar nomination, told from inside the bombers' dilemma.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the two friends, the recruitment, the ordinary morning before the plan. Abu-Assad films the bombers as people, not symbols. Notice how the film refuses to offer easy judgment.

name: Mohsen Makhmalbaf
teaser: Makhmalbaf was imprisoned as a teenager for anti-Shah activity — after the revolution he became Iran's most radical filmmaker, making Kandahar and The Cyclist.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — an Afghan refugee cycling in circles for money, his audience watching. Makhmalbaf films endurance as spectacle. Notice how the crowd becomes a mirror of the world that watches refugees suffer.

name: Jafar Panahi
teaser: Panahi was banned from filmmaking for 20 years by the Iranian government — he kept making films anyway, smuggling them out on flash drives, and they kept winning prizes.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the hospital, the woman in labor, the sisters. Panahi's film follows women in Tehran in a chain of escapes. Notice how each woman's story hands off to the next without a break.

name: Asghar Farhadi
teaser: Farhadi won two Oscars for Best Foreign Film — A Separation and The Salesman — and his films turn Iranian middle-class life into moral thrillers.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the divorce petition, the argument in the judge's chamber, the split. Farhadi's genius is that both sides are right. Notice how every character's choice is reasonable — and disastrous.

name: Majid Majidi
teaser: Majidi's Children of Heaven is the story of a boy who loses his sister's shoes — it became Iran's first Oscar-nominated film and a worldwide favorite.

exploreAction.targetName: Children of Heaven (1997), the first 25 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the shoe repair, the loss, the shared secret. Majidi films poverty with warmth, not misery. Notice how the film's gentle humor never lets the hardship feel heavy.

name: Bahram Beyzai
teaser: Beyzai's Bashu, the Little Stranger — about a war-traumatized boy adopted by a woman who doesn't speak his language — is considered a masterpiece of Iranian cinema.

exploreAction.targetName: Bashu, the Little Stranger (1986), the first 25 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the bombed village, the boy running, the woman who takes him in. Beyzai films a friendship built without a shared word. Notice how language becomes the film's subject, not just its medium.

name: Kim Ki-duk
teaser: Kim Ki-duk's Spring, Summer, Fall, Winter... and Spring is set on a floating monastery — a cycle of seasons telling the whole arc of a human life.

exploreAction.targetName: Spring, Summer, Fall, Winter... and Spring (2003), the first 25 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the floating temple, the monk and the boy, the animal cruelty. Kim films each season as a stage of life. Notice how the lake's stillness becomes the film's moral frame.

name: Lee Chang-dong
teaser: Lee was South Korea's culture minister before returning to filmmaking — his Burning, based on a Murakami story, was Korea's first Oscar shortlist for Best Foreign Film.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the delivery, the cat that may not exist, the greenhouse speech. Lee builds a mystery where even the mystery is uncertain. Notice how the film makes you question what you saw.

name: Hong Sang-soo
teaser: Hong makes the same film every year — two or three people, soju, walks, and conversations — and each one is somehow a revelation. He's the minimalist king of Korean cinema.

exploreAction.targetName: The Day He Arrives (2011), the first 25 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the filmmaker arriving, the drinking, the walking. Hong's zooms and pans are so simple they're radical. Notice how the film's repetitions — same streets, same soju — become its meaning.

name: Im Kwon-taek
teaser: Im made over a hundred films in a career spanning five decades — his Chunhyang is a pansori (Korean opera) brought to cinema, and he won Best Director at Cannes.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the pansori singer on stage, the audience, the story beginning. Im intercuts the live performance with the film's reenactment. Notice how the opera's emotion is doubled by the cinema.

name: Na Hong-jin
teaser: Na's The Chaser is a serial-killer thriller that's really about a failed detective chasing his own mistakes — the film announced a new master of Korean genre cinema.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the pimp, the missing girls, the chase that keeps missing. Na builds suspense by letting you know the killer's identity early. Notice how the film's violence is sudden, ugly, and quick.

name: Kim Jee-woon
teaser: Kim's A Tale of Two Sisters is Korea's most celebrated horror film — a psychological ghost story where the ghost might be the protagonist herself.

exploreAction.targetName: A Tale of Two Sisters (2003), the first 25 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the sisters' return home, the stepmother, the first strange night. Kim's horror is about family wounds, not jump scares. Notice how the house's spaces rearrange themselves without explanation.

name: Ann Hui
teaser: Hui was part of Hong Kong's New Wave — her A Simple Life, about an aging servant and the man she cared for, won her the best director award at Venice.

exploreAction.targetName: A Simple Life (2011), the first 25 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the servant collapsing, the decades of care, the quiet bond. Hui films a lifetime of service with respect. Notice how the film's small daily scenes accumulate into a whole life.

name: Johnnie To
teaser: To made Election and its sequel in a year each — the films are about triad elections, and To directed them like thrillers about boardroom politics.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the triad election, the two candidates, the dragon head. To films organized crime as corporate warfare. Notice the stillness: his violence is sudden, formal, and almost balletic.

name: Stephen Chow
teaser: Chow went from Hong Kong TV comedy to directing Kung Fu Hustle — a $20 million martial arts comedy that became the highest-grossing Chinese-language film of its time.

exploreAction.targetName: Kung Fu Hustle (2004), the first 25 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the tenement, the gangs, the landladies who turn out to be kung fu masters. Chow blends Looney Tunes physics with wuxia grace. Notice how every gag is also a fight and every fight is also a gag.

name: Fruit Chan
teaser: Chan's Made in Hong Kong follows three teenagers at the end of the handover era — the film was shot on leftover film stock and won prizes everywhere.

exploreAction.targetName: Made in Hong Kong (1997), the first 25 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the rooftop, the letters, the three lost kids. Chan films the city's last colonial summer. Notice the grainy, near-documentary texture — that's leftover stock and real streets.

name: Stanley Kwan
teaser: Kwan's Rouge is a ghost story about a 1930s courtesan who returns to modern Hong Kong to find her lost love — the film made Anita Mui a legend.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the ghost descending into the modern city, the past in color. Kwan films the 1930s in sumptuous reds and the present in muted blues. Notice how the romance is already a ghost before the film begins.

name: Ringo Lam
teaser: Lam's City on Fire — about an undercover cop and a thief who bond before discovering who they are — directly inspired Tarantino's Reservoir Dogs.

exploreAction.targetName: City on Fire (1987), the first 25 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the undercover setup, the jewelry store, the two strangers who become friends. Lam films the friendship before the betrayal. Notice the warehouse standoff's setup — it rhymes with a later famous film.

name: Andrew Lau
teaser: Lau co-directed Infernal Affairs, the Hong Kong thriller that Scorsese remade as The Departed — the original is often considered the better film.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the two moles, the parallel lives, the meeting on the rooftop. Lau cuts between cop and gangster with perfect symmetry. Notice how the film's identity theme is set in the very first scenes.

name: Alan Mak
teaser: Mak co-directed Infernal Affairs with Andrew Lau — the film's script, about moles on both sides of the law, won every major Hong Kong award.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how the film sets up its two protagonists as mirror images — one cop undercover in the mob, one mobster undercover in the police. Notice the handshake scene: identity exchange in one gesture.

name: Carlos Saura
teaser: Saura directed Carmen, Blood Wedding, and El Amor Brujo — his flamenco trilogy turned dance into cinema and made him Franco-era Spain's great metaphorist.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the dance studio, the rehearsal, the flamenco that becomes a love story. Saura films rehearsal as performance and performance as life. Notice how the camera is part of the choreography.

name: Víctor Erice
teaser: Erice made only three features in his career — each one took decades — and each is a quiet masterpiece. The Spirit of the Beehive is about a girl who meets the ghost of Frankenstein.

exploreAction.targetName: The Spirit of the Beehive (1973), the first 25 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the village, the beehouse, the girl watching Frankenstein. Erice films Franco's Spain through a child's eyes: everything is half-seen. Notice how the film's silence is its terror and its beauty.

name: Pedro Costa
teaser: Costa has spent decades filming the same Lisbon slum, Fontainhas — his In Vanda's Room is shot on digital video over months, blurring fiction and documentary.

exploreAction.targetName: In Vanda's Room (2000), the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the dark room, the two women, the long takes. Costa films the slum's daily life as if it were holy. Notice how the film's darkness is not darkness of mood but of place — real, lived shadow.

name: José Luis Guerín
teaser: Guerín's In the City of Sylvia follows a man searching for a woman he barely remembers — the film is an essay about looking, made of glances.

exploreAction.targetName: In the City of Sylvia (2007), the first 25 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the café terrace, the notebook, the faces passing. Guerín's film is almost silent: it's about the act of watching. Notice how the film teaches you to look the way its hero looks.
